question: However a badminton shuttlecock leaves the racket, even tumbling or struck at an odd angle, within a fraction of a second it is flying cork-first and stays that way. What about its design makes this happen?
correct_answer: Heavy cork in front, feather drag behind
alternative_answers: Weight at the front, air resistance at the back
Centre of mass is in the cork, drag is in the feathers
It works like an arrow or a dart: nose heavy, tail draggy
The feathers act as a stabilising skirt behind the heavy cork
headline_answer: Heavy cork in front, feather drag behind
source_excerpt: Regardless of initial orientation, it will turn to fly cork first, and remain in the cork-first orientation.

extra.verification_notes: The shuttlecock's heavy cork base and high-drag feather skirt make it aerodynamically stable and self-orienting cork-first, matching the claimed answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttlecock).

explanation: The cork base is far heavier than the feather skirt, so the shuttle's centre of mass sits right at the front. The wide cone of feathers, meanwhile, produces most of the air resistance, and that drag acts behind the centre of mass. Whenever the shuttle is sideways, the air pushes the light, draggy tail back behind the heavy nose, exactly like the fletching on an arrow or the flights on a dart. The effect is so strong that the shuttle self-corrects almost instantly, which is why badminton players can hit it from any angle without it ever arriving feathers-first.

question: The longest tennis match ever played was a first-round match between John Isner and Nicolas Mahut at Wimbledon in 2010. Over how many days was it played?
source_excerpt: 11 hours and 5 minutes over three days.

extra.why_interesting: Players know it was 'the longest match ever' but picture one very long afternoon; the answer reveals the match outlived the days it was scheduled in.
extra.verification_notes: Isner–Mahut (2010) was played over three days (22–24 June) and remains the longest tennis match; no longer match has been recorded.

explanation: Play was suspended for darkness twice, and the fifth set alone finished 70 games to 68, taking longer than any complete match before it.

question: In golf, one under par on a hole is a birdie and two under is an eagle. What is the name for the far rarer score of three under par?
source_excerpt: A hole played three strokes under par. Also albatross.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has heard 'birdie' and 'eagle'; the stem gives the ladder and the player has to reach for the rare top rung, which is a big seabird.
extra.verification_notes: Albatross is a standard term for three under par; 'double eagle' is a synonym, so accept both.

explanation: It is also called a double eagle in America, and it is rarer than a hole-in-one because it almost always needs a holed second shot on a par five.

question: In 1971, during the Apollo 14 mission, which astronaut became the only person ever to hit golf balls on the Moon?
source_excerpt: Shepard struck two golf balls, driving the second, as he jokingly put it, 'miles and miles and miles'.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes astronauts were all business; the answer is a man who smuggled a club head into his spacesuit pocket, and it is the first American in space.
extra.verification_notes: Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14 (Feb 1971), and no one has done so since; no crewed lunar landing has occurred since 1972.

explanation: Shepard, the first American in space, swung one-handed in his stiff suit and joked that the second ball went for 'miles and miles' in the low gravity.

question: The fastest recorded tennis serve is roughly 263 kilometres per hour. Which racket sport beats that comfortably, with smashes officially clocked at over 400 kilometres per hour?
source_excerpt: India's Satwiksairaj Rankireddy broke a decade-old Guinness world record for the fastest shot ever in badminton with an astonishing 565 km/hour smash.

extra.why_interesting: The player reaches for tennis or squash as the 'fast' sport; the gentle garden game turns out to launch the fastest projectile in all racket sports.
extra.verification_notes: Guinness-recognised badminton smash records are 565 km/h (Rankireddy, 2023) and 438 km/h (women's), both over 400 km/h, and the tennis serve record of ~263 km/h still stands.

explanation: The shuttlecock leaves the racket at extreme speed but its feathers brake it almost instantly, which is why rallies are still playable.

question: Tennis balls were traditionally white. Yellow balls were introduced to help television viewers follow the ball, but tradition-bound Wimbledon only adopted them in which year?
source_excerpt: Tennis balls of the 'optic yellow' colour were not introduced into Wimbledon until 1986.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume yellow balls have 'always' been standard, or guess the 1970s when colour TV arrived; Wimbledon held out until well into the 1980s.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources say Wimbledon first used optic yellow balls in 1986, although the ITF approved yellow in 1972; I did not open the Wikipedia page.

explanation: The international federation approved yellow balls in 1972, but Wimbledon kept white ones for another fourteen years before giving in.

question: In the year 2000, which sport made its ball two millimetres bigger, from 38 to 40 millimetres, deliberately slowing the game so spectators and television cameras could keep up?
source_excerpt: more viable as a televised spectator sport

extra.why_interesting: A sport deliberately handicapping its own ball sounds absurd until you realise the rallies had become too fast for cameras and spectators.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the ITTF changed the ball from 38mm to 40mm in October 2000 to slow the game for TV viewers, and the size has not changed since.

explanation: The larger, slower ball was introduced just after the Sydney Olympics, and the sport later also switched from celluloid to plastic balls.

question: Three of golf's four major championships move between different courses each year. Which major is always played at the same course?
source_excerpt: Unlike the other major tournaments which change host venues with each tournament, the Masters is always held at the same host venue: Augusta National Golf Club

extra.why_interesting: The stem's footholds let any casual fan reason it out: the one major with a permanent home is also the one with the famous green jacket.
extra.verification_notes: The Masters is always held at Augusta National, unlike the other three men's majors, which rotate venues (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_Tournament).

explanation: It has been held at Augusta National in Georgia since 1934, which is why its azaleas and the winner's green jacket are so instantly recognisable.

question: Despite decades of campaigning, squash has never been an Olympic sport. At which Games will it finally make its Olympic debut?
source_excerpt: The 2028 Summer Olympics will include the sport of squash for the first time as an optional sport.

extra.why_interesting: A sport with a century-old professional circuit and world championships never made the Olympics; the player has to work out which upcoming Games finally lets it in.
extra.verification_notes: Squash is confirmed for its Olympic debut at LA 2028 (men's and women's singles, July 15-24, 2028) and has never been in the Games before, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squash_at_the_2028_Summer_Olympics

explanation: The International Olympic Committee approved squash in 2023 alongside cricket, lacrosse and flag football for the Los Angeles programme.

question: Only one tennis player in history has won all four Grand Slam singles titles and Olympic gold in the same calendar year. Who did it in 1988?
source_excerpt: German tennis player Steffi Graf achieved what no one else had done before or has done since.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Serena Williams, Federer or Djokovic as the greatest ever, yet none of them managed this; the answer is a teenager from 1988.
extra.verification_notes: Graf remains the only player to win all four Slams plus Olympic gold in one calendar year (1988); no Olympics since could have changed this.

explanation: Graf was just 19, and 1988 was the first time tennis had returned as a full Olympic sport since 1924, so the chance did not even exist for earlier champions.

question: Padel, the enclosed-court racket sport booming across Europe, was invented in 1969 by a man who built a court at his holiday home. In which country?
source_excerpt: Corcuera modified his squash court to incorporate elements of platform tennis.

extra.why_interesting: Padel is so dominated by Spain and Argentina that almost everyone guesses Spain; its real birthplace is a holiday home on the Pacific coast of Mexico.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Enrique Corcuera invented padel in 1969 in Acapulco, Mexico, and reports no competing origin claim.

explanation: Enrique Corcuera built the first walled court in Acapulco, and a Spanish friend took the idea home to Marbella, which is how Spain became its heartland.

question: Which tennis player won the French Open men's singles title a record fourteen times, more than most all-time greats have won across all four Grand Slams combined?
source_excerpt: Nadal won 92 ATP Tour singles titles, with 22 major titles—including a record 14 French Open titles.

extra.why_interesting: The sheer number is the hook: fourteen titles at a single Grand Slam is more than most all-time greats win in total across all four.
extra.verification_notes: Nadal's record 14 French Open men's singles titles is confirmed by Wikipedia, and nothing found suggests it has been matched or surpassed.

explanation: Nadal lost only four matches in his entire career at Roland Garros, and his statue now stands at the entrance to the grounds.

question: Both are the oldest championships in their sports. Which one was held first: the Wimbledon tennis championships, or golf's Open Championship?
source_excerpt: The first Open Championship took place on October 17, 1860 at Prestwick Golf Club in Scotland.

extra.why_interesting: Wimbledon's heavy tradition makes it feel like the ancient one, but golf's Open had already been running for seventeen years when the first Wimbledon was played.
extra.verification_notes: The first Open Championship was held in 1860 at Prestwick, 17 years before the first Wimbledon in 1877 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Open_Championship).

explanation: The Open was first played at Prestwick in Scotland in 1860, while Wimbledon did not begin until 1877, when it was staged to raise money for a lawn roller.

question: For most of tennis history the balls were white. What invention in people's living rooms persuaded the sport to switch to bright yellow in the 1970s?
source_excerpt: In 1972, the International Tennis Federation introduced yellow balls... easier to see on television.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume yellow balls are simply tradition, but the colour was chosen for a household appliance, not for the players on court — and it was broadcasters, not athletes, who drove the change.
extra.verification_notes: Yellow balls were introduced by the ITF in 1972 to be more visible on (colour) television, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_ball; no newer events contradict this.

explanation: Research showed white balls were hard to follow on colour TV screens, so the sport adopted optic yellow in 1972, though Wimbledon stubbornly kept white balls until 1986.

question: Until 1986, Wimbledon still used white tennis balls, long after other tournaments had switched to yellow. The change was made for the benefit of people who were not on the court at all. Who were they?
source_excerpt: Tennis balls of the 'optic yellow' colour were not introduced into Wimbledon until 1986.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume yellow tennis balls are simply what tennis balls have always been, or that the colour helps the players. In fact white balls were standard for a century, and the change was made for people watching at home, not for anyone on court — and Wimbledon resisted it for fourteen years.
extra.verification_notes: Yellow balls were introduced for TV visibility (ITF 1972) and Wimbledon adopted them in 1986; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_ball

explanation: Yellow balls were approved in 1972 because they showed up far better on colour television, but tradition-bound Wimbledon held out for another fourteen years before switching.
